pages.title: Artemis IV - NASA
pages.description: NASA is targeting the first Artemis lunar landing in early 2028. After launching the crew aboard the Orion spacecraft, they will transfer to a commercial lunar lander for transport to the surface of the Moon. Lander readiness will determine which provider will safely carry them to the surface and back to Orion in lunar orbit before the crew returns home aboard Orion—splashing down safely in the Pacific Ocean.

These fossils were preserved within expanding and contracting wetlands between 100,000-12,500 years ago. Many of the Pleistocene animals of Tule Springs are still alive today, including the coyote ( Canis latrans ), jackrabbit ( Lepus sp.), and aquatic snails. Some animals went extinct, disappearing from North America entirely. Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 1: Columbian Mammoth The Columbian mammoth is the largest and most identified extinct large mammal found in the Las Vegas Formation at Tule Springs Fossil Bed National Monument. Columbian mammoths belonged to the same family as living elephants. Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) history and heritage include experiences of people with cultural, religious, and linguistic traditions from India, China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Vietnam, Hawai’i, Samoa, Tonga, among other nations from Asia and the Pacific Islands. It is impossible to tell the experiences of these various groups with a single history. The breadth of Asian American and Pacific Islander experience is a vital aspect of America's rich and diverse past. El cartel se ha de exhibir en un sitio conspicuo donde los empleados y los solicitantes de empleo lo puedan ver. Se tiene que exhibir un cartel en todo sitio de empleo aunque no haya ningún empleado elegible en él. Se pueden procurar ejemplares del cartel preparado por el Departamento (WH 1420SP) para su información o para colgar en el sitio de empleo. Éstos se pueden imprimir a color con un impresor a color o con una versión blanca y negra. Se recomiendan impresores con 1 MB de memoria por lo menos. Para imprimir un ejemplar, favor de seguir estas instrucciones: Se puede disponer de este archivo sólo en el formato PDF. Para ver y/o imprimir documentos en PDF, ha de tener un programa que lea ese tipo de archivo (e.g., Adobe Acrobat Reader® v5 ) y que esté a su alcance en su sitio de trabajo. Pulse en el enlace para el cartel de la Ley de Ausencia Familiar y Médica y espere hasta que salga en pantalla. Para imprimir, pulse sobre el icono (dibujito) que representa el impresor ya adentro del Acrobat Reader. No seleccione la opción de imprimir que aparece en el navegador. Close b-jazz Mapper since: May 07, 2017 Last map edit: November 16, 2026 My Story One of things I like to do when meeting new mappers is ask them how they discovered and started contributing to OSM. Well my story goes back to the very, very early days of OSM. I heard about it through some forums (I don’t even remember which) and took a look at it. To say that the tools were in their infancy would be an understatement. There were no aerial images to make use of, things were mostly done through GPS tracks. Living in the heart of Silicon Valley, there were already some roads mapped out. There were areas right where I lived that were definitely wrong, but the tools just weren’t there for me to invest time, so I walked away for several years. Many years later, I was doing some geocaching in my spare time and there was a big stink when geocaching.com moved from Google maps to OSM. At the time, I didn’t get why they would do that. (A while later it became painfully obvious as I realized that Google was charging through the nose for high traffic users of their services.) I didn’t really pick up OSM at that time either. Add another year or two and I saw that Strava had switched from Google to OSM as well and I really started to be more aware that OSM was becoming more and more mainstream. When I retired in 2017, I wanted to have a project to work on so I started learning OSM and finding more and more ways to contribute. Close b-jazz's Diary Cleaning up Golf Courses in the United States Posted by b-jazz on 3 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 4 November 2026. Written 2025-10-30… Published 2026-11-03 About three years ago, during my day-to-day mapping activities, I came across a golf course that had some obvious errors. I didn’t think much of it at the time. Just a fairway that was drawn right across the top of a green. But the more golf courses I looked at, the more frequently I encountered this error. I soon learned about a golf course simulator video game that was built on OpenStreetMap data and was attracting a large influx of simulator enthusiasts who weren’t seasoned OSM mappers. Along with that came various tools to aid in converting OSM data into these simulators, as well as tutorial videos that made some very bad assumptions about how golf courses should be mapped. These factors set the stage for some very bad mapping practices to spread around the world. My understanding is that attempts were made to correct these bad habits at the source, but the tutorial author wasn’t interested in revising or removing his video. Combine that with YouTube’s bad decision to hide down votes on videos, and you’re left with de facto training material that is widely disliked but that new golf course mappers have no way of knowing is a poor source of truth. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. (Photo by the Bureau of Land Management) A routine patrol across public lands near Yuma, Arizona, can change in an instant. Eric Cole knows that better than most. Cole, a supervisory law enforcement ranger with the Bureau of Land Management’s Yuma Field Office , was once called into the desert after another hiker found an unconscious woman and called 911. She had apparently suffered an allergic reaction to an insect bite and, by the time Cole reached her, also appeared to be suffering from heat-related illness. pages.text: Billions of T. rex likely roamed the Earth, paleontologists report | National Geographic Paleontologists figured out how many T. rex lived on Earth—and they found that about 20,000 would have been alive at any given time during a two- to three-million year timespan. Illustration by STOCKTREK IMAGES, Nat Geo Image Collection SCIENCE NEWS Billions of T. rex likely roamed the Earth, paleontologists report The iconic predator’s estimated abundance means the T. rex fossils we have today are exceedingly rare. By Michael Greshko Published April 19, 2021 • 6 min read If you traveled back in time 67 million years ago to ancient Montana, you’d be entering the realm of a tyrant: the iconic predator Tyrannosaurus rex . Before you venture into that lost world, though, you might want to know: On average, how close is the nearest T. rex to you? That might sound like an impossible thing to know—but after crunching through two decades’ worth of T. rex research, a new study provides estimates of the animal’s population density. In all likelihood, a T. rex would be within 15 miles of you, if not much closer. The new study, published last Thursday in Science , also translates these population densities into estimates for how many T. rex ever lived. On average, researchers estimate that some 20,000 T. rex lived at any one time and that about 127,000 generations of the dinosaurs lived and died. Those averages imply that a total of 2.5 billion T. rex lived in the species’ native North America, possibly as far north as Alaska and as far south as Mexico, over a two- to three-million-year timespan.

They are an essential part of American history and embody the strong and resilient characteristics of the American people - so much so that they were designated as our National Mammal in 2016. Once numbering ~30 million and ranging across the United States and in Canada and Mexico, bison were hunted to near extinction, with only several hundred remaining by the 1870’s. Through ongoing conservation work, bison are recovering from a low of fewer than 1,000 individuals. Today, 19 herds in 12 states roam the American Plains.
